name: Eggs (egg yolk)
lead: Whole eggs and egg yolks are among the most widely eaten foods in physique-focused communities. Lifters and looksmaxxers use them as an inexpensive, calorie-dense source of complete protein, fat and choline to support muscle gain, hard training and a fuller, leaner-looking physique. A hard-boiled chicken egg supplies roughly 12.6 g of protein, 10.6 g of fat and 294 mg of choline per 100 g, and egg protein scores the maximum on the PDCAAS protein-quality scale.[1]

The chain people describe is straightforward: eggs make it easier to reach daily protein and calorie targets, those targets feed training and recovery, and consistent training builds muscle. Yolk fat and nutrients (choline, B12, riboflavin, vitamin D, lutein) are also discussed as part of general nutrition that supports energy, skin and hair.[1][22][25]

On forums such as looksmax.org and T Nation, members describe anything from two eggs a day to well over a dozen, cooked or raw, inside bulking plans, high-protein routines and 'animal-based' diets.[2][3][4] Raw-egg drinking, a long-standing strongman and bodybuilding trope, is a recurring thread topic, and members debate whether it is nutritious, a meme, or a food-safety question.[16][18][19]

Research on eggs spans cardiovascular outcomes, cholesterol, muscle protein synthesis, weight control and infant allergy. A 2020 BMJ analysis of three large US cohorts plus an updated meta-analysis found that up to one egg a day was not associated with cardiovascular disease in the general population,[7] and a randomized trial in young men found whole eggs stimulated post-exercise muscle protein synthesis more than egg whites with the same protein content.[8]

angle.text: Eggs are used as a convenient protein and fat source in bulking and cutting diets, helping people reach daily protein and calorie targets for building muscle. Whole-egg eaters in lifting communities also cite the yolk's choline, vitamins and fats as part of the appeal.

infobox: About 10.6 g per 100 g, mostly in the yolk[1]
About 294 mg per 100 g; yolks are among the richest dietary sources[1][22]
About 51% bioavailable raw vs about 91% cooked[1]

paras: Per 100 g, a hard-boiled chicken egg contains about 155 kcal, 10.6 g fat and 1.12 g carbohydrate, along with 12.6 g protein, vitamin B12 (about 46 percent of the Daily Value), riboflavin (about 38 percent), vitamin D, vitamin A, phosphorus and choline (about 53 percent).[1] The white is about 90 percent water and 10 percent protein with almost no fat, while the yolk holds most of the lipid, along with much of the choline and the pigment lutein.[1][25] A medium to large 50 g egg supplies about 70 kcal and 6 g of protein.[1]

Choline is an essential nutrient used to build cell membranes, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and the methyl donor trimethylglycine. The US National Academy of Medicine set adequate intakes of 550 mg per day for adult men and 425 mg for adult women in 1998, and a single large hard-boiled egg provides about 147 mg.[22] Symptomatic deficiency is described as rare but can involve fatty liver and muscle damage.[22]

Lutein, which gives yolk its yellow colour, is a carotenoid that animals obtain from plant feed; it concentrates in the macula of the eye, and poultry feed often includes carotenoids to colour yolks.[25] A systematic review of 141 studies on plant-based and meat-eating diets noted that animal foods including eggs, dairy, poultry and fish supply nutrients such as vitamin B12, which was generally lower in vegetarians and vegans.[9]

sections.h: Use in training and physique diets
paras: Lifters count eggs as a cheap, quick-cooking way to add protein and fat. In the common bulking pattern, eggs sit alongside rice, oats, meat and dairy to reach a calorie surplus; in cutting phases, whole eggs or egg whites supply protein with controlled calories. A 50 g egg carries about 6 g of protein for about 70 kcal.[1]

Whole eggs versus egg whites is a long-running gym debate. A randomized trial in young men reported that after resistance exercise, whole eggs stimulated muscle protein synthesis more than an equal amount of protein from egg whites alone, a result frequently cited by yolk-eating lifters.[8] A multicenter trial in the International Journal of Obesity examined an egg breakfast within a weight-loss diet, a setting relevant to leaner-physique goals.[10]

In T Nation training logs, members describe days built around many whole eggs and extra yolks alongside meat and shrimp, and others discuss yolks in connection with insulin response and training energy.[11][12] On looksmax.org, some members say eggs are a staple they eat daily despite disliking the taste, and others argue chicken delivers more protein per calorie.[3][4][6]
Some looksmax.org members build eggs into animal-based diets, arguing for fish, meat and fat over dairy and processed foods, while others argue for avoiding eggs and dairy altogether.[21]

Drinking raw eggs has a long association with strength culture. Looksmax.org threads include members recounting mornings of 13 to 16 raw eggs, or asking how to ferment them.[16][17][18] Others call the practice a meme.[19]

Nutrition sources describe two points that bear on the practice. First, only about 51 percent of raw egg protein is bioavailable, compared with about 91 percent for cooked egg, so cooked protein is absorbed nearly twice as well.[1] Second, raw egg white contains avidin, a protein that binds the vitamin biotin very tightly; heat reduces its activity, and a 1991 assay found activity remaining after frying or poaching but complete inactivation only after boiling for more than four minutes.[23] Biotin is involved in hair, skin and nail health, and researchers in the 1920s and 1930s linked heavy raw-egg-white feeding in animals to hair loss, dermatitis and neurological signs, a pattern named egg-white injury; György showed in 1941 that avidin was responsible.[23][24]

Salmonella is the other recurring concern. Wikipedia cites a 2002 USDA study estimating that about 2.3 million of 69 billion US eggs a year, roughly 1 in 30,000, were contaminated; cooking to 71 C kills the bacteria instantly, and health authorities typically advise against eating raw eggs.[1] A food-microbiology study modelled Salmonella growth in unpasteurized liquid whole egg, yolk and white.[15] In-shell pasteurization and the UK Lion scheme, in which hens are vaccinated against Salmonella, are described as risk-reduction measures.[1]

A single egg contains about 186 mg of cholesterol (373 mg per 100 g), which made eggs a target of dietary advice for decades. The 1977 US Senate committee report Dietary Goals for the United States recommended cutting cholesterol intake to 300 mg a day, a recommendation that drew criticism from some scientists and food industry groups at the time.[26]

Studies since have been inconsistent. In 2013 one meta-analysis found no link between eggs and heart disease or stroke while another associated four eggs a week with 6 percent higher cardiovascular risk; a 2018 meta-analysis of randomized trials found eggs raised total, LDL and HDL cholesterol versus no eggs but not versus low-egg diets; and two 2020 meta-analyses plus an umbrella review found no association at moderate intake in the general population.[1] Wikipedia notes that some findings in people with type 2 diabetes pointed to higher risk with more than one egg a day, and that observational studies can be affected by confounding.[1]

The 2020 BMJ study pooled the Nurses' Health Study, Nurses' Health Study II and Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, with up to 32 years of follow-up, and reported that at least one egg per day was not associated with incident cardiovascular disease; the authors noted that higher egg eaters tended to have higher BMI and eat more red meat.[7]

A 2025 randomized cross-over trial of 61 adults separated the effects of egg-derived dietary cholesterol from saturated fat on LDL cholesterol, motivated by suggestions that saturated fat has the larger influence.[13] A 2023 meta-analysis of prospective studies associated substituting plant-based foods, including nuts, for eggs with lower cardiometabolic risk.[14] Gut bacteria convert the choline in egg phosphatidylcholine into trimethylamine and then TMAO, a compound linked in some studies to atherosclerosis; Wikipedia's choline article reports that choline intake itself has not been shown to raise cardiovascular death, and that the TMAO association may reflect confounding such as kidney dysfunction.[1][22]

Egg is among the most common food allergies in infants, and egg white reactions are more frequent than yolk reactions.[1] The PETIT trial tested a two-step egg introduction in high-risk infants with eczema in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design.[20]

Biotin supplements are marketed for hair and nails; Wikipedia states that randomized trials in healthy adults have not shown hair benefits, while deficiency can cause hair thinning, brittle nails and a facial rash.[24] Lutein from eggs and other foods is studied for eye health, with a 2013 AREDS2 formulation reported to reduce progression of age-related macular degeneration.[25]

No studies found on egg yolk specifically for appearance outcomes such as skin or hair. Egg research that touches physique includes the whole-egg versus egg-white muscle protein synthesis trial in young men and the egg-breakfast weight-loss trial.[8][10] Wider egg research concerns cardiovascular risk, LDL cholesterol and allergy prevention in infants.[7][13][20]

The egg carton is invented in Smithers, British Columbia.[1]

lore.intro: Eggs come up on looksmax.org and T Nation as a cheap staple, a source of energy, a raw-food experiment and an argument about protein efficiency.[2][5][6][11]

claims.claim: Eating eggs gives noticeably more energy the next day
claims.believers: One poster says 2 eggs leave him with 'way more energy' the next day, and that he feels the benefits strongly despite disliking the taste.[5]
claims.experts: No published study has tested next-day energy from egg intake in healthy adults; eggs supply protein, fat, B vitamins and choline.[1]

claims.claim: Eggs are a poor protein source per calorie compared with chicken
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster who ate 16 eggs (about 99 g protein, 1,144 kcal) argued chicken thigh or breast would give 1.5 to 3 times the protein for the calories.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists about 12.6 g protein and 155 kcal per 100 g of hard-boiled egg and a maximum PDCAAS score for egg protein.[1]

claims.claim: Whole eggs are better than egg whites for building muscle
claims.believers: Lifters on T Nation log meals of many whole eggs plus extra yolks as part of mass-building diets.[11]
claims.experts: A randomized trial in young men found whole eggs produced greater post-exercise muscle protein synthesis than egg whites with the same protein.[8]

claims.claim: Raw eggs are as nutritious or more so than cooked
claims.believers: Members post about drinking 13 to 16 raw eggs in a sitting, and ask how to ferment them.[16][17][18]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports raw egg protein is about 51 percent bioavailable versus about 91 percent cooked, and that raw eggs carry a salmonella risk.[1]

claims.believers: Some looksmax.org members argue for avoiding eggs and dairy in favour of fish, meat and fat.[21]
claims.experts: A 2020 BMJ analysis of three US cohorts found at least one egg per day was not associated with incident cardiovascular disease.[7]

claims.claim: Raw eggs are a strength-building tradition
claims.believers: Members post about drinking 13 to 16 raw eggs in a sitting.[18]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports only about 51 percent of raw egg protein is bioavailable, and that raw egg white contains avidin that binds biotin.[1][23]

claims.claim: Yolks are the nutrient-rich part and egg whites alone miss out
claims.believers: Whole-egg lifters point to the yolk's choline, B12, fats and lutein.[11]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports the yolk holds most of the fat and much of the choline, and the 2017 trial found whole eggs outperformed whites for muscle protein synthesis.[1][8]

claims.claim: Dietary cholesterol from eggs is the main driver of LDL
claims.believers: Traditional guidance, such as the 1977 Dietary Goals, set a 300 mg daily limit.[26]
claims.experts: A 2025 randomized cross-over trial was designed around suggestions that saturated fat has the greater influence on LDL.[13]

card.summary: A staple protein-and-choline food; its appearance relevance is mostly indirect.

quick.overview:
Eggs are an everyday food that provide protein, fat and choline. They appear in muscle-building and general diet discussions.

No published trials were found testing egg yolk specifically for skin, hair or other appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Eggs supply complete protein and nutrients such as choline and B vitamins as part of the overall diet.
quick.risks: Research on dietary cholesterol is mixed; several meta-analyses found no link to heart disease at moderate intake. Raw eggs can carry salmonella, and egg allergy is common in infants.
